The Lesser yellowlegs (Tringa flavipes) is a medium-sized shorebird that undertakes long migrations between its Arctic breeding grounds and wintering areas ranging from the southern United States to southern South America. Field studies have documented that eggs are incubated for a period of 23 days [ab = 23 days] at an average nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and upon hatching, these precocial chicks are able to leave the nest almost immediately. The hatchlings emerge with a wet weight of 11.5 grams [Wwb = 11.5 grams], a mass that supports their rapid development in the short Arctic summer. Feather growth proceeds quickly, with the downy young achieving the capacity for sustained flight at 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching] when maintained under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (41 °C [T = 41 °C]). This relatively brief developmental period is an adaptation to the constrained window of resource availability in their breeding habitat.

The ultimate adult body mass attained by female Lesser yellowlegs has been measured at 80.65 grams [Wwi = 80.65 grams], placing them among the smaller members of the genus Tringa. This mass is achieved during the boreal summer when prey items such as insects, crustaceans, and small fish are abundant on the tundra. Females tend to be slightly heavier than males on average, a pattern often observed in charadriiforms where females invest considerable energy into egg production. The species exhibits a single annual reproductive cycle, with females producing exactly one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a strategy that, given the short Arctic summer, limits total annual reproductive output to a level typical of long-lived scolopacids.

Sexual maturation in the Lesser yellowlegs is not immediate upon reaching adult body size; instead, individuals attain puberty at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] when maintained at 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This timing means that young birds are reproductively mature within the same breeding season in which they hatched, though whether they actually attempt to breed in their first summer is influenced by a suite of ecological constraints. The onset of gonadal activity coincides with the completion of the prebasic molt and acquisition of definitive plumage. Delayed reproduction until the second year of life is a common strategy among many migratory scolopacids, allowing young birds to build sufficient fat reserves and migratory experience before undertaking the energetic demands of both long-distance migration and successful nesting. The alignment of these developmental schedules with the short Arctic breeding season is critical for population persistence.

The first successful nesting attempt by a Lesser yellowlegs typically occurs at typically 365 days after hatching [tR = typically 365 days after hatching] when measured at 41 °C [T = 41 °C], which places the event in the spring of the bird's second calendar year. This one-year delay between hatching and initial reproductive output is a common life-history pattern among medium-sized shorebirds that winter in the Southern Hemisphere. During this interval, juveniles migrate south, overwinter, and return north, accumulating the physiological condition necessary for egg formation and territory defense. The reproductive output per clutch is approximately four eggs [N_R_i = per clutch is approximately four eggs], and with a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], the species maintains a modest annual fecundity. Brood parasitism has not been documented in this species, and both parents share incubation and chick-rearing duties, which further constrains the annual fecundity.

Longevity records for the Lesser yellowlegs indicate a maximum lifespan of 4.7 years in the wild according to banding records from the Animal Diversity Web, though some analyses suggest a potential lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] under optimal conditions at 41 °C [T = 41 °C]. This discrepancy likely reflects differences between average field mortality and the physiological ceiling of the species. Survival rates are influenced by habitat loss on both breeding and wintering grounds, exposure to environmental contaminants, and the inherent risks of migration. The reproductive lifespan is therefore limited to perhaps a decade in the most successful individuals, during which they can produce a maximum of ten to twelve offspring over their lifetime given the constraint of a single clutch per year. Understanding these demographic parameters is essential for conservation planning, as the species is listed as a species of high concern in several North American shorebird conservation plans.
